summary: The moat rests on an architecture choice (containerised inspection microservices) and multi-cloud breadth, both copyable. The scarce asset, current threat signatures, belongs to incumbent firewall vendors with installed base and distribution. VMware owns the hypervisor insertion point; cloud providers own the native control plane. Some switching cost once policy embeds, but not enough.

objections.objection: The most likely copier, Palo Alto Networks (or Check Point/Fortinet), already has the hard part: a mature threat-signature feed and research team, a virtualised firewall, and the enterprise firewall relationship. Re-packaging VM-Series as autoscaled containers with a segmentation policy UI is an engineering project, not a new capability; the concept itself names this as the riskiest assumption.
objections.evidence: concept:riskiest_assumption.assumption; concept:build.hardest_parts ("Keeping threat definitions current", "Competing with incumbent network security vendors"); concept:competitors (Palo Alto Networks VM-Series)

objections.objection: Threat definitions are a content moat that runs against the startup: incumbents amortise signature research across perimeter, cloud and endpoint customers. A new entrant must either build a research team (cost, lag) or license feeds, which leaves inspection quality as a commodity it does not control.
objections.evidence: concept:mvp.features[1] ("Deep packet inspection with threat definitions"); concept:build.hardest_parts

objections.objection: Platform owners control the insertion points. VMware NSX owns east-west traffic in the hypervisor and can add or partner for L7 inspection; AWS/Azure security groups are free and improving. The startup depends on APIs of the very vendors who can bundle the feature, so its integration depth is borrowed, not owned.
objections.evidence: concept:competitors (VMware NSX, cloud-native security groups); concept:risks; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html ("There is no additional charge for using security groups")

objections.objection: Differentiation is stated as architecture and breadth (containerised, elastic, cloud-agnostic). These are design choices incumbents can adopt within a product cycle and are close to 'better UX' rather than data or network effects; nothing compounds with more customers.
Pure segmentation players (Illumio, Guardicore) could add inspection or partner with a firewall vendor, squeezing the startup from the other side; the combination itself is not protected.

strongest_point: Once application-aware policy is discovered and embedded in DevOps pipelines across several clouds, ripping it out is painful; that policy graph is a real switching cost.
what_would_change_my_mind: Benchmarks showing incumbent virtual firewalls cannot reach east-west throughput/cost parity even when re-packaged as containers.
Proof-of-concept customers who chose it over extending their incumbent firewall contract.
A proprietary east-west traffic dataset that measurably improves detection with each added customer.
An OEM or strategic partnership giving privileged insertion into a major private-cloud platform.
